name: italian-basics

description.en: 120 Italian words and phrases for beginners: numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, ten family members, ten greetings and polite phrases, yes and no, 20 everyday nouns, six adjectives and 16 verbs. The front shows the Italian word, nouns with their definite article (il libro, lo zio, la casa; l' with the gender added: l'acqua (f.)); the back gives the English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number. Notes give genders, plurals and feminine forms. From Wikidata's lexemes and the US Foreign Service Institute's Italian Programmed Course (public domain), checked against Italian, English and Swedish Wiktionary and Folkets lexikon.
description.sv: 120 italienska ord och fraser för nybörjare: talen 0–20, tiotalen och 100, veckodagarna, månaderna, åtta färger, tio familjemedlemmar, tio hälsningar och artighetsfraser, ja och nej, 20 vardagliga substantiv, sex adjektiv och 16 verb. Framsidan visar det italienska ordet, substantiv med bestämd artikel (il libro, lo zio, la casa; l' med genus angivet: l'acqua (f.)); baksidan ger betydelsen på engelska och svenska, eller siffrorna för ett tal. Anteckningar anger genus, plural och femininformer. Från Wikidatas lexem och amerikanska Foreign Service Institutes Italian Programmed Course (fri från upphovsrätt), kontrollerat mot italienska, engelska och svenska Wiktionary och Folkets lexikon.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Word list. A candidate list of 120 words and phrases for a first Italian course was drawn up by hand from the brief's categories (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and polite phrases; everyday nouns; adjectives; verbs), choosing the most basic word for each concept and following the authored French deck where the languages allow. The family has ten members, uncle and aunt included, so that lo (lo zio) appears on a card. No frequency list or textbook word list was copied.

Wikidata lexemes. SPARQL query 1 fetched every Italian lexeme (language Q652) whose lemma is a candidate (plus buon giorno, buona sera, buona notte, per piacere, scusa, arancio and tavolo, looked at as alternatives), with its category, gender (P5185), senses, English and Italian glosses and sense items (P5137). Four candidates were not found: buonasera, a presto, per favore and scusi. The lexeme search (API calls 2) found no lexeme for buonasera, buona sera, a presto, per favore, per piacere, mi scusi or buon giorno; it found the verb scusare (L1206184), whose form F44 is scusi (third person singular, present imperative). The full JSON of all lexemes found was fetched with API calls 3. For each word the lexeme of the card's part of speech was chosen (numeral for numbers, noun for nouns, days and months, adjective for colours and adjectives, verb for verbs, interjection or adverb for the greetings, sì and no).

Wikidata items. The items linked from the chosen senses (P5137), plus four items found with the item search (API calls 5: 17 Q40118, good evening Q19279366, goodbye Q2506912, thank you Q19279214), were fetched with API calls 4 (labels and aliases in it, en, sv and mul). They gave the English and Swedish names of days, months, colours, family members, greetings and everyday things and the digit labels of the numbers. For colours the adjective lexeme gives the front and the feminine form, and the noun lexeme of the same colour links the item (most adjective lexemes have no senses). The labels of the grammatical items used in the lexemes (categories, genders, form features) were fetched with API call 6.

Phrases from the FSI course. For the phrases with no Wikidata lexeme, the Internet Archive was searched for public-domain Foreign Service Institute Italian courses (call 8). The two searches found the Italian (Programmed) Course, Volume I (1976), with a public-domain licence, one audio lesson of the FSI Italian FAST course, and other items that were not used (lending-library scans titled "Italian : programmed" and an ERIC Post Language Program course of unknown status). The OCR text of the Programmed Course was downloaded (call 9) and searched with grep (call 10); passages were then read in context by line range. The course gives buon giorno and buona sera (Recapitulation, Greetings), per favore and per piacere (Unit XXII), arrivederci and arrivederLa (Unit XXII), come sta? (Unit XVII), prego (Unit XXIV), scusi (Unit XXIV), the word for thank you (Unit XVII; written g in the course's abbreviations) and si/no (Unit VIII). It has no ciao, buonanotte or a presto. A presto (see you soon), on the first word list, has neither a Wikidata lexeme nor a public-domain source and was replaced by come sta? (how are you?), which the course teaches. The quotations from the course give its text with OCR errors and spacing normalised (for example "bsne" read as bene); where that matters the evidence says so.

Writing the cards. The front is the Italian word as in the lexeme's lemma (or the FSI phrase), lower case. Nouns are preceded by the definite article that shows their gender: il and lo (before z, s + consonant, gn and ps) for masculine nouns, la for feminine ones; before a vowel the article is written l' and the gender is added in brackets, m. or f. (l'acqua (f.), l'uomo (m.), l'amico (m.)); the apostrophe is the straight ASCII apostrophe. Days and months are given without an article and in lower case, as Italian writes them, with their gender in a note. Colours and adjectives are given in the masculine singular with the feminine in a note; verbs in the infinitive. Greetings are given in their one-word spelling where Wikidata has that lemma (buongiorno, buonanotte) and, for buonasera, as the FSI course's buona sera written as one word in the same way as Wikidata's lemmas buongiorno (L1165742) and buonanotte (L1165741), a spelling that Italian and English Wiktionary only confirm; the two-word spellings (buon giorno, buona sera, buona notte, as the FSI course writes them) are named in the notes. The back is our own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits (tagged zxx, as digits are in no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item exists and has them; otherwise they are the usual equivalents, chosen by the authors and checked in English Wiktionary, Folkets lexikon and Swedish Wiktionary. Where a word has two everyday equivalents both are given (buongiorno: good morning, good day; ciao: hi, bye; città: city, town; andare: gå, åka; parlare: tala, prata). Rule for text not given by a content source: English and Swedish equivalents and the facts behind the notes come from the authors' own knowledge of the languages, are worded by the authors and are only confirmed in the verification sources; such single words and short facts of usage count as the authors' own content. Per favore is snälla, the usual Swedish word in a spoken request (Folkets lexikon gives it for the interjection please); the Swedish note adds that a spoken Swedish request often ends with tack.

Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and is confirmed by a source: the gender of each day and month (domenica is the only feminine day); the feminine of each colour and adjective (blu invariable, verde, grande and arancione the same in the feminine; buon before most masculine nouns); the plural, with its article (i, gli, le), of every countable noun, from the lexeme's forms and the Wiktionary head lines (irregular: gli uomini, le mani, le città unchanged; i fratelli also meaning brothers and sisters, i figli children, i nonni grandparents); mano being feminine; lo before z, s + consonant, gn and ps; l'amica; uno also being the article before z, s + consonant, gn and ps, and sei also meaning you are (each with a front note "number"); the formal and informal forms (arrivederLa, come stai?, scusa), per piacere, prego to let someone go ahead, non before a verb, and the Swedish gå/åka distinction. Notes are our own wording.

Cross-checking. Every Italian word was looked up in Italian Wiktionary (calls 12), except come sta?, which has no page there, and no, whose entry gives only marginal senses (English Wiktionary, Wikidata and the FSI course check those two): spelling, part of speech, the gender mark on the head line against the article on the card, the plural, and the first relevant definition (quoted in each card's evidence). Every English meaning was checked against the Italian section of English Wiktionary (calls 13, REST definition API), and for nouns, adjectives, days and months the Italian head template in the page's wikitext (gender, plural, inflection). Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (call 15), English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match, and, where a page with an Italian section exists, in Swedish Wiktionary (calls 14). A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quote is what the source returned, with wiki markup removed; quotations longer than 160 characters are cut and marked with "…". The raw responses and scripts were working files and are not published.

Dictionaries not used. The brief suggested Treccani or the Accademia della Crusca for checking the Italian. Treccani's terms (https://www.treccani.it/footer/termine-condizioni/, read before any dictionary page) state: "Ai sensi dell'art. 4 della Direttiva UE 2019/790, si comunica che l'uso di tutti i contenuti presenti sul portale www.treccani.it per attività di text e data mining è espressamente vietato senza preventiva autorizzazione scritta del titolare dei diritti." Treccani was therefore not consulted at all; its home page (https://www.treccani.it/) was fetched only to find the link to these terms. The Accademia della Crusca publishes no general dictionary to check words against; only its home page (https://accademiadellacrusca.it/) was fetched, which shows "© 2019 Accademia della Crusca" and no licence, and it was not used. Italian Wiktionary and English Wiktionary, whose licences allow automated use, verify every Italian form and gender instead.

Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (the Italian, English and Swedish label or alias of each linked item that matches the card's text, and the mul digit label of each number: 251 checks on 98 items) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (scripts/validate_sources.ts).

Excluded: a presto (no open source, see step 5), words with two equally common forms or meanings that a single card cannot separate (il tavolo and la tavola, both table; la strada and la via, both street; azzurro beside blu; marrone and castano for brown), the formal/informal pronouns tu and Lei (which need grammar, not a flashcard; they appear only in notes), the year (anno and annata), and conoscere/sapere (both to know).
selection: 120 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, orange); ten family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother, uncle, aunt); ten greetings and polite phrases (buongiorno, buonasera, buonanotte, ciao, arrivederci, come sta?, grazie, per favore, prego, scusi) and yes and no (sì, no); 20 everyday nouns (house, water, bread, milk, apple, book, chair, door, window, dog, cat, city, school, man, woman, friend, hand, day, night, week); six common adjectives (grande, piccolo, buono, cattivo, nuovo, vecchio); and 16 common verbs in the infinitive (essere, avere, andare, fare, venire, parlare, mangiare, bere, amare, volere, potere, vedere, leggere, scrivere, dormire, lavorare). The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list or textbook. Every word has a Wikidata lexeme except buonasera, come sta? and per favore, which come from the public-domain FSI course. Left out: a presto (no open source; come sta? took its place), table and street (two everyday words each: tavolo/tavola, strada/via), brown (marrone, castano) and the light blue azzurro, the pronouns tu and Lei, the pair anno/annata, and conoscere/sapere. Nouns are given with the definite article (il, lo, la); before a vowel the elided l' is followed by the gender, (m.) or (f.); the notes give the plural with its article (i, gli, le) for every countable noun. Colours and adjectives are given in the masculine singular, with the feminine in a note. Days and months are given without an article and in lower case, as Italian writes them; their gender is in a note on every day and month card. Greetings are written as one word (buongiorno, buonasera, buonanotte), with the two-word spelling in the note.

rounds.summary: Every card has evidence from a content source (Wikidata, or the FSI course for buonasera, come sta? and per favore) and at least two verification sources. Italian Wiktionary agrees with the spelling of every Italian word on the cards except the phrase come sta?, which it has no page for (English Wiktionary does); the gender shown on every noun, day and month card agrees with the Wikidata lexeme (or its forms), Italian Wiktionary and the English Wiktionary head template. English Wiktionary confirms every English back; Folkets lexikon, Swedish Wiktionary or a Swedish Wikidata label confirms every Swedish back. The builder's Wikidata checks cover the Italian, English and Swedish labels or aliases of 97 linked items (249 checks), including the digit label of every number; they all pass. Discrepancies between sources and how they were resolved are listed below. No independent review round has been run yet.

findings.issue: The brief named Treccani or the Accademia della Crusca for checking the Italian. Treccani's terms reserve text and data mining under article 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 and forbid it without written permission; the Crusca publishes no general dictionary and its site states no licence.
findings.resolution: Neither was used: Treccani's terms were read before any dictionary page was requested, and no Treccani or Crusca dictionary content was fetched (method, step 9). Italian Wiktionary and English Wiktionary, whose licences allow it, verify every Italian form and gender instead.

findings.issue: The first word list had a presto (see you soon), but no open content source gives it: no Wikidata lexeme or item, and the public-domain FSI Programmed Course does not contain it.
findings.resolution: Replaced by come sta? (how are you?), which the FSI course teaches with its meaning and formality (Unit XVII).

findings.issue: The FSI course writes buon giorno and buona sera as two words; Wikidata's lexemes are buongiorno and buonanotte (one word), and Wikidata has no lexeme for buonasera in either spelling.
findings.resolution: The cards use the one-word spellings (Wikidata's lemmas; for buonasera the Italian Wiktionary entry), and every note names the two-word spelling, which English Wiktionary lists as an alternative spelling of each.

findings.issue: The sense of the lexeme nove (L5162-S1) has the Italian gloss "numero ordinale per 9" and links two items: Q28469719 (ninth, the ordinal) and Q19108 (9). Nove is the cardinal number; the ordinal is nono.
findings.resolution: The card uses Q19108 (mul label "9", Italian alias "nove"); Italian Wiktionary (numero cardinale) and English Wiktionary (Numeral: nine) confirm the cardinal. Recorded here for Wikidata's editors.

findings.issue: The sense of diciassette (L1201799-S1) links no item.
findings.resolution: Q40118 (17) was found with the item search (call 5); it has the mul label "17" and the Italian alias "diciassette", which the checks use.

findings.issue: The lexeme sessanta (L1201863) has the lexical category adjective, while the other number lexemes are numerals.
findings.resolution: No effect on the card (lemma and item are right); recorded here.

findings.issue: The lexeme mano (L640238) has the gender feminine, but its form F1 "mano" is tagged masculine and F2 "mani" feminine.
findings.resolution: The card says la mano and the note says it is feminine, as the lexeme's gender statement, Italian Wiktionary (f sing) and English Wiktionary ({{it-noun|f|…}}) say. Recorded here for Wikidata's editors.

findings.issue: The lexeme amico (L72273) has no gender statement (P5185); its forms are tagged masculine (amico, amici) and feminine (amica, amiche).
findings.resolution: The masculine gender on the card comes from the forms, Italian Wiktionary (m sing) and English Wiktionary ({{it-noun|m|f=+…}}).

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label for day (Q573) is "dygn" (a 24-hour period), not "dag".
findings.resolution: Kept "dag", the everyday word, confirmed by Folkets (day → dag) and Swedish Wiktionary (giorno → dag). No Swedish label check for Q573.
